title: Revisiting 'Blade Runner 2049': A Visual and Philosophical Marvel

commenti.body:
I'm in the minority of viewers in that I just plain old didn't enjoy it.

I have enormous respect for Villeneuve's mastery of visual storytelling, and every shot of the movie is purposeful and gorgeous; so like, don't let this come across as me being the naysayer. There's a whole lot there to love, and the craftsmanship is remarkable. It's remarkable enough that I see nothing wrong with folks who enjoy it for that reason even if nothing else.

But as a story, it just falls entirely flat for me. There's nothing there that I felt any connection to, no characters who I enjoyed watching, no plot element that I found myself invested in seeing through. As a sci-fi experience, it's closer to something like Peter Watts' novels, in that I feel the story is projected *at* me as an exploration of ideas rather than inviting me into it to think and feel. And again, there's an audience--a huge audience!--for those kinds of stories. Peter Watts is a very beloved author in the same way that *Blade Runner 2049* is a hugely popular film. But somehow I find myself disappointed to not be part of that target audience.

I wish I could see it with the original score by Jóhann Jóhannsson. I mean, I don't think he was actually finished before he was replaced. Anyway, I love what Hans Zimmer did, but certainly compared to the original his score lacks nuance, subtlety, and variety. I mean, those are big words, I know - I'm nitpicking, don't get me wrong. And it may or may not have been the right choice for the film, I love it as it is. 

My only real gripes would be the ending action scene in the water which does fall a little bit flat. But that's okay. And Leto's Niander Wallace is very, very broad. It does work, I suppose? But I feel like perhaps a Mads Mikkelsen would have chosen a much more nuanced and interesting characterization. Or, again, I wish I could've seen Bowie's Wallace. I'm sure he would've been wonderful. 

Fantastic film and a great theater-going experience as well.
I think much of the audience that enjoys the movie was able to emotionally connect with it in some way.
Totally agree on the water scene and Leto! What would you say about Harrison Ford's performance?

Blade Runner 2049 totally caught me off guard on my first viewing. I watched it on an airplane and despite the poor viewing medium I was totally surprised by how much I loved it. I’ve since watched it several more times (not on the airplane) and it has become one of my all time favorites.   

What sets 2049 apart from other sc fi and modern movies is its visual and thematic cohesiveness. Joi’s translucence and intangibility are amazing modes in which Villeneuve conveys themes regarding not only her character as an individual but also as a couple with K. I continually ask myself if she really did feel those rain drops on her fingers or if she really did feel love for K in her last moments with him. This of course is all aided by how stunning the effects are in 2049 and how seamlessly they are incorporated. 

Another good example of this is K’s car. Did you ever question why K’s car has wheels if it can fly, me neither, because it just makes sense. The world feels gritty and analogue despite its futuristic setting. K’s car is totally worn in, the screens are scuffed, and K inhabits it like I would my 2007 Subaru. If K is an android  one might expect his tech to be maintained meticulously, so when the question of his birth origins is presented these details aid our belief that he may be the one. So much of 2049 feels like a spectacle but never takes its eye off of its characters. I heard some say that what made David Lean’s epics such as Lawrence of Arabia , Bridge on the river kwai so amazing was his ability to move characters through a story without losing the small moments in the spectacle. I feel this is also true of blade runner 2049 and Villeneuve’s work in general. This is also what I believe will be 2049s impact on modern cinema, a perfect marriage of practical and CG effects that not only allow for spectacle but also enhance character moments. 



The themes of 2049 are presented through so many avenues that you could watch it a hundred times and still find new perspectives to ruminate on.

Overall I'd say he's quite good in it. You know, it's not a very flashy role and of course, it could've only been him, really. So he's kind of got it easy, haha. I suppose that's why I felt a little disappointed that he wasn't a little more animated in the ending, but to be fair that's as much a fault of the script and setting as anything. And you know, he's a man of a certain age. His brawl with Gosling I thought was great though, and he's great in the scene with CGI Sean Young, too.
I didn’t find it difficult to emotionally connect with some of the characters.

Johansson managed to completely finish the score, but his work was rejected by the film producers based on the results of focus groups - they decided to take a safer, commercial path - to take the more famous Zimmer with the same Yamaha synthesizer as Vangelis. Johannson recorded twenty musical themes for the film, sooner or later they will leak onto the Internet (now you can only hear samples of the first five tracks) [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cZtDaVxxAWI](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cZtDaVxxAWI)
